rv.q: The ride it offers is as smooth as it is wistful.
But d espite some moving moments that explore the idea of missed cosmic connections, The Coast Starlight too often feels like you're on a trip to nowhere.
It's an almost impossible concept to describe and by all rights it shouldn't work -- except that it does, casting a spell unlike anything I've experienced in a theatre recently.
What Keith Bunin does in The Coast Starlight is astonishing.
The Coast Starlight is the sort of play that will stick in your mind long afterward.

With an excellent ensemble cast, ingenious set, and an empathy-quotient that feels like a balm in the current climate, this is a train journey that will inspire and delight the most reluctant travelers.
Tyne Rafaeli’s direction is also a kinetic marvel.

Bunin’s play lets us hear their inner thoughts – and, most importantly, the conversations they could (and should) have had with each other, which are alternately revealing, quite funny, and, as often as not, deeply sad.
Bunin is a thought provoking playwright, however this production, directed by Tyne Rafaeli feels verbose, and lacking movement.
However, The Coast Starlight chugs along at a snail’s pace.
The writing, directing, set design, costumes, and acting all come together and meld in a magic evening that completely defines why we go to the theater.
The lyrical, Wilder-evoking dénouement owes as much (and perhaps more) to the exquisite Lincoln Center Theater production, directed by Tyne Rafaeli, as to Bunin’s writing.

cn.t: Critics find this train journey drama a mostly pleasant ride, praising the ensemble cast and empathetic tone, though some feel the pace lags and the experimental structure doesn't fully deliver on its premise.
